We show that bigger and better models exhibit more human-like concept organization, across four families of language models and three knowledge graph embeddings.

papers.title: Cross-neutralising: Probing for joint encoding of linguistic information in multilingual models
papers.research_question: How are linguistic properties encoded jointly across typologically-similar languages in multilingual models like M-BERT and XLM-R?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that multilingual models jointly encode typological linguistic properties across languages, and this can be probed using the cross-neutralising method.
papers.conclusion: Typological feature values are encoded jointly across languages in multilingual models and can be localized via language centroids.
papers.key_findings:
Self-neutralising by subtracting language centroids removes typological information, reducing probing accuracy to chance levels.
Cross-neutralising shows that performance deteriorates for languages sharing the same typological feature value, indicating joint encoding.
This joint encoding pattern is observed in both M-BERT and XLM-R models.
The effect is consistent across different layers of the models.
Language centroids capture specific feature values in a localizable way across languages.
papers.limitation: When probing performance before neutralising is low (<75% accuracy), it is unclear what information the language centroids capture, limiting the interpretation of results.
future_direction: Correlate typological feature encoding with downstream task performance
Use cross-neutralising for selective generalization in models based on typology
Apply the method to other scenarios like multimodal models
papers.abstract: Multilingual sentence encoders are widely used to transfer NLP models across languages. The success of this transfer is, however, dependent on the model's ability to encode the patterns of cross-lingual similarity and variation. Yet, little is known as to how these models are able to do this. We propose a simple method to study how relationships between languages are encoded in two state-of-the-art multilingual models (i.e. M-BERT and XLM-R). The results provide insight into their information sharing mechanisms and suggest that linguistic properties are encoded jointly across typologically-similar languages in these models.

papers.title: Prometheus Mind: Retrofitting Memory to Frozen Language Models
papers.research_question: How can memory be retrofitted to a frozen pretrained language model without architectural changes or weight modification, and in a fully reversible manner?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that memory can be retrofitted to a frozen language model using 11 modular adapters (7% parameter overhead) that are fully reversible, by solving four key problems: extraction via Contrastive Direction Discovery, reliable stage-wise training, zero-training injection via Identity V (lm_head.weight), and fixing hidden state collapse via learned projections.
papers.conclusion: Memory can be retrofitted to frozen language models without architectural changes using modular, reversible adapters, and the principles of CDD, stage-wise training, Identity V, and hidden state projection provide a pathway for adding capabilities to frozen models.
papers.key_findings:
Contrastive Direction Discovery (CDD) can extract semantic directions (subject, verb, object, temporal) from transformer hidden states without labeled data by contrasting minimal pairs.
Stage-wise training of each adapter on simple proxy tasks succeeds where end-to-end joint optimization collapses.
Using the model's own lm_head.weight rows as value vectors (Identity V) for memory injection requires no training and generalizes to any token in the vocabulary, whereas learned value encoders fail to generalize.
Transformer hidden states collapse semantically distinct concepts (e.g., 'wife' vs 'brother' have 0.98+ cosine similarity), but a projection trained to match embed_tokens similarities can recover distinction (0.98→0.09).
The system achieves 94.4% retrieval accuracy on clean inputs with only 530MB (7%) of adapter parameters added to a frozen Qwen3-4B model.
papers.limitation:
All experiments use a single base model (Qwen3-4B); transfer to other model families is not validated.
No evaluation on standard memory benchmarks such as LoCoMo or BABILong.
Partially learned routing: while all decision boundaries are learned, the composition logic (control flow) remains in Python.
Testing limited to 88 entities; scaling behavior is unknown.
Injection layer sensitivity: the layer 35 (97% depth) injection point was empirically tuned; theoretical understanding is lacking.
Single-token injection: current implementation injects one token at a time; multi-token answers require extension.
future_direction: Validating the approach on other model families.
Evaluation on standard memory benchmarks (LoCoMo, BABILong).
Investigating the theoretical basis for Identity V and injection layer selection.
papers.abstract: Adding memory to pretrained language models typically requires architectural changes or weight modification. We present Prometheus Mind, which retrofits memory to a frozen Qwen3-4B using 11 modular adapters (530MB, 7% overhead) -- fully reversible by removing the adapters. Building this system required solving four problems: (1) Extraction -- we develop Contrastive Direction Discovery (CDD), which finds semantic directions via minimal pairs without labeled data. (2) Training -- end-to-end optimization collapses; stage-wise training of each adapter on simple proxy tasks succeeds. (3) Injection -- learned encoders fail to generalize; we find that lm_head-weight rows already provide the mapping we need, requiring no training. (4) Hidden state collapse -- transformers make ``wife'' and ``brother'' 0.98+ similar; we train projections to recover distinction (0.98 $\rightarrow$ 0.09). On PrometheusExtract-132 (132 cases), the system achieves 94.4% retrieval on clean inputs (n=54, 95% CI: [84.9%, 98.1%]), degrading to 19.4% on informal inputs with ellipsis, filler words, or implicit subjects (n=36). The primary bottleneck is relation classification (47.3% accuracy), responsible for most extraction errors.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Understanding of Propositional Logical Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models internally perform propositional logical reasoning? What computational strategies do they employ?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a coherent computational architecture for propositional logical reasoning in Qwen3 models, comprising four interlocking mechanisms: Staged Computation, Information Transmission, Fact Retrospection, and Specialized Attention Heads.
papers.conclusion: The investigation uncovers a coherent computational architecture for propositional logical reasoning, with four interlocking mechanisms that generalize across model scales, rule types, and reasoning depths, suggesting fundamental computational strategies rather than task-specific shortcuts.
papers.key_findings:
The model organizes reasoning into staged computation: early layers process facts, middle layers process logical expressions, and late layers aggregate for prediction.
Information transmission occurs through segment-terminal tokens (boundary tokens) that act as information hubs.
Fact retrospection: the model persistently re-accesses source fact tokens throughout the network depth.
Specialized attention heads: splitting heads (early layers), transmission heads (middle layers), and fact-retrieval heads (middle to late layers) implement the above mechanisms.
These mechanisms generalize across model scales (8B and 14B), rule types (11 categories), and reasoning depths (one-hop and two-hop).
papers.limitation:
The internal computations within MLP layers remain largely unexplored.
The analysis does not explain how or when these mechanisms emerge during training.
Cannot definitively rule out that these patterns reflect sophisticated statistical shortcuts rather than genuine logical algorithms.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to deeper reasoning chains (i.e., three-hop and beyond).
Investigating diverse model architectures beyond the Qwen family (e.g., Llama, Mistral, etc.).
Analyzing training dynamics to reveal how and when these mechanisms emerge during pretraining.
papers.abstract: Understanding how Large Language Models (LLMs) perform logical reasoning internally remains a fundamental challenge. While prior mechanistic studies focus on identifying taskspecific circuits, they leave open the question of what computational strategies LLMs employ for propositional reasoning. We address this gap through comprehensive analysis of Qwen3 (8B and 14B) on PropLogic-MI, a controlled dataset spanning 11 propositional logic rule categories across one-hop and two-hop reasoning. Rather than asking ''which components are necessary,'' we ask ''how does the model organize computation?'' Our analysis reveals a coherent computational architecture comprising four interlocking mechanisms: Staged Computation (layer-wise processing phases), Information Transmission (information flow aggregation at boundary tokens), Fact Retrospection (persistent re-access of source facts), and Specialized Attention Heads (functionally distinct head types). These mechanisms generalize across model scales, rule types, and reasoning depths, providing mechanistic evidence that LLMs employ structured computational strategies for logical reasoning.

papers.title: Just-in-time and distributed task representations in language models
papers.research_question: When are transferrable task representations formed in language models during in-context learning, and how do they change over the context?
papers.core_contribution: Transferrable task representations in language models evolve non-monotonically and sporadically, activating only at key tokens, while a persistent representation of task identity is maintained throughout the context.
papers.conclusion: Language models form multiple types of task representations during in-context learning, with transferrable representations activating sporadically and task identity persisting, revealing a complex and nuanced dynamic of the model's internal state.
papers.key_findings:
Transferrable task representations (e.g., task vectors) accrue evidence from multiple in-context examples but form sporadically and non-monotonically.
Task identity representations are robustly decodable from residual activations across most tokens in the context, persisting throughout.
Transferrable task representations exhibit strong temporal locality, forming effectively only at specific tokens (e.g., the colon token before answer generation).
In longer- and mixed-generation tasks, transferrable task representations often decay over output units, showing semantic locality and limited task scope.
For complex tasks requiring state tracking or combining distinct subtasks, effective task representations are more distributed across tokens.
papers.limitation:
Zero-shot recontextualization remains challenging for tasks that require intermediate-state tracking or more complicated computation.
Overriding token activations at intermediate layers with task vectors may cause the model to lose task state information formed in earlier layers.
future_direction: Study the mechanistic bases for the strong temporal and scope locality observed in models' in-context transferrable task representations.
papers.abstract: Many of language models' impressive capabilities originate from their in-context learning: based on instructions or examples, they can infer and perform new tasks without weight updates. In this work, we investigate when representations for new tasks are formed in language models, and how these representations change over the course of context. We study two different task representations: those that are ''transferrable'' -- vector representations that can transfer task contexts to another model instance, even without the full prompt -- and simpler representations of high-level task categories. We show that transferrable task representations evolve in non-monotonic and sporadic ways, while task identity representations persist throughout the context. Specifically, transferrable task representations exhibit a two-fold locality. They successfully condense evidence when more examples are provided in the context. But this evidence accrual process exhibits strong temporal locality along the sequence dimension, coming online only at certain tokens -- despite task identity being reliably decodable throughout the context. In some cases, transferrable task representations also show semantic locality, capturing a small task ''scope'' such as an independent subtask. Language models thus represent new tasks on the fly through both an inert, sustained sensitivity to the task and an active, just-in-time representation to support inference.

papers.title: Dissecting Recall of Factual Associations in Auto-Regressive Language Models
papers.research_question: How do auto-regressive language models internally retrieve factual associations during inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a three-step internal mechanism for factual attribute extraction in auto-regressive LMs, involving subject enrichment by early MLPs, relation propagation, and attribute extraction by attention heads.
papers.conclusion: Factual associations are stored in lower layers and extracted by MLP sublayers to form attribute-rich subject representations; upon a query, the attribute is extracted by MHSA sublayers whose parameters often encode subject-attribute mappings.
papers.key_findings:
Critical information flows from relation and then subject positions to the prediction via specific attention edges.
Subject representations are enriched with multiple attributes by early MLP sublayers.
Attribute extraction is primarily performed by upper MHSA sublayers via attention heads that encode subject-attribute mappings.
The extraction mechanism is a three-step process: subject enrichment, relation propagation, and attribute extraction.
Approximately 70% of predictions use this extraction mechanism.
papers.limitation:
Projections to vocabulary space are an approximation, especially in early layers.
Attention knockout may have information leakage across positions, though blocking a range of layers alleviates this.
future_direction: knowledge localization
model editing
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models (LMs) are known to capture factual knowledge in their parameters. While previous work looked into where factual associations are stored, only little is known about how they are retrieved internally during inference. We investigate this question through the lens of information flow. Given a subject-relation query, we study how the model aggregates information about the subject and relation to predict the correct attribute. With interventions on attention edges, we first identify two critical points where information propagates to the prediction: one from the relation positions followed by another from the subject positions. Next, by analyzing the information at these points, we unveil a three-step internal mechanism for attribute extraction. First, the representation at the last-subject position goes through an enrichment process, driven by the early MLP sublayers, to encode many subject-related attributes. Second, information from the relation propagates to the prediction. Third, the prediction representation "queries" the enriched subject to extract the attribute. Perhaps surprisingly, this extraction is typically done via attention heads, which often encode subject-attribute mappings in their parameters. Overall, our findings introduce a comprehensive view of how factual associations are stored and extracted internally in LMs, facilitating future research on knowledge localization and editing.

papers.title: A Joint Matrix Factorization Analysis of Multilingual Representations
papers.research_question: How do multilingual language models encode morphosyntactic features in their layers? Are the findings robust in low-resource settings? How do morphosyntactic typology and downstream task performance relate to the factorization outputs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a joint matrix factorization analysis tool for comparing multilingual and monolingual representations, and uses it to study morphosyntactic feature encoding across 33 languages and 17 categories, finding variations across layers and language properties.
papers.conclusion: The introduced tool provides insights into language representation in multilingual models and has practical implications for improving performance in cross-lingual tasks. Future work will extend the analysis to multimodal models.
papers.key_findings:
Encoding of morphosyntactic information varies across upper and lower layers, with category-specific differences influenced by language properties such as writing system and number of unique characters.
Logographic writing systems (Chinese, Japanese) lead to distinct representations and present unique challenges for multilingual models.
Multilingual representations show distinct encoding patterns in subsets of languages with low language proximity.
Representation of low-resource languages benefits from the presence of related languages.
Factorization outputs yield a phylogenetic tree structure similar to linguists' trees and correlate with cross-lingual task performance.
papers.limitation:
Only used RoBERTa and XLM-R, not other models like BERT, mBERT, T5, mT5 due to computational resources.
Downsampled Wikipedia to 200MB per language, though validated with a public XLM-R checkpoint.
Analyses limited to morphosyntactic features, plan to expand to semantics and pragmatics.
future_direction: Extend the analysis tool to examine representations learned by multimodal models.
Expand the analysis to other linguistic aspects, such as semantics and pragmatics.
papers.abstract: We present an analysis tool based on joint matrix factorization for comparing latent representations of multilingual and monolingual models. An alternative to probing, this tool allows us to analyze multiple sets of representations in a joint manner. Using this tool, we study to what extent and how morphosyntactic features are reflected in the representations learned by multilingual pre-trained models. We conduct a large-scale empirical study of over 33 languages and 17 morphosyntactic categories. Our findings demonstrate variations in the encoding of morphosyntactic information across upper and lower layers, with category-specific differences influenced by language properties. Hierarchical clustering of the factorization outputs yields a tree structure that is related to phylogenetic trees manually crafted by linguists. Moreover, we find the factorization outputs exhibit strong associations with performance observed across different cross-lingual tasks. We release our code to facilitate future research.

papers.title: The Geometry of Multilingual Language Model Representations
papers.research_question: How do multilingual language models maintain a shared multilingual representation space while still encoding language-sensitive information in each language?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that multilingual language models encode information along orthogonal language-sensitive and language-neutral axes, facilitating feature extraction for downstream tasks and cross-lingual transfer learning.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual language models encode features along orthogonal language-sensitive and language-neutral axes, enabling targeted extraction of features for downstream tasks and cross-lingual transfer learning.
papers.key_findings:
Languages occupy similar linear subspaces after mean-centering, as shown by causal effects on language modeling performance and direct subspace comparisons.
Subspace means differ along language-sensitive axes that encode information such as token vocabularies, and shifting representations by language means is sufficient to induce token predictions in different languages.
Stable language-neutral axes encode information such as token positions and part-of-speech, and these axes are orthogonal to language-sensitive axes.
The identified axes (both language-sensitive and language-neutral) are relatively stable across middle layers of the model.
Token position information is encoded along nonlinear structures like spirals, toruses, and curves in the representation space.
future_direction: Investigate how nonlinear structures (e.g., spirals, toruses) arise from and interact with the dot product self-attention mechanism in Transformer models.
Conduct a more detailed analysis of how specific representational structures are retained across layers.

Assess how multilingual language models encode more complex linguistic features geometrically, and the extent to which representation spaces can be fully decomposed into orthogonal subspaces encoding different features.
papers.abstract: We assess how multilingual language models maintain a shared multilingual representation space while still encoding language-sensitive information in each language. Using XLM-R as a case study, we show that languages occupy similar linear subspaces after mean-centering, evaluated based on causal effects on language modeling performance and direct comparisons between subspaces for 88 languages. The subspace means differ along language-sensitive axes that are relatively stable throughout middle layers, and these axes encode information such as token vocabularies. Shifting representations by language means is sufficient to induce token predictions in different languages. However, we also identify stable language-neutral axes that encode information such as token positions and part-of-speech. We visualize representations projected onto language-sensitive and language-neutral axes, identifying language family and part-of-speech clusters, along with spirals, toruses, and curves representing token position information. These results demonstrate that multilingual language models encode information along orthogonal language-sensitive and language-neutral axes, allowing the models to extract a variety of features for downstream tasks and cross-lingual transfer learning.

papers.title: When Meanings Meet: Investigating the Emergence and Quality of Shared Concept Spaces during Multilingual Language Model Training
papers.research_question: How do shared, language-agnostic concept spaces emerge and develop during the multilingual pretraining of large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Shared concept spaces emerge early in multilingual pretraining and remain relatively stable, but alignment with these spaces is language-dependent and influenced by training data composition.
papers.conclusion: Shared concept spaces emerge early and are progressively refined during multilingual pretraining, with alignment depending on language and data composition. Targeted multi-aligned data can improve alignment for low-resource languages.
papers.key_findings:
Shared concept spaces arise early in pretraining and continue to refine throughout training.
Alignment with shared concept spaces depends on language similarity and training data proportion.
Cross-lingual concept patching can shift model behavior, such as selecting dominant senses for polysemous words or translating cross-lingual homographs instead of copying them.
The model initially prefers copying input words over translating them, a behavior learned early.
Patching from averaged representations across languages (the 'seen' setting) is often as effective as patching from English-only representations for inducing concepts in English output.
papers.limitation:
Focuses primarily on a single, relatively small model (EuroLLM-1.7B), though provides supporting evidence on two others.
Analysis is restricted to nouns; behavior of other word classes is not studied.
Inherits biases from the Multi-SimLex dataset, such as ambiguous translations for polysemous words.
Focuses only on the simple task of word-level translation; findings may not generalize to more complex tasks.
future_direction: Investigate how representations for other word classes (beyond nouns) behave.
Study the emergence and behavior of language-agnostic spaces for more complex multilingual tasks like sentence-level translation or reasoning.
papers.abstract: Training Large Language Models (LLMs) with high multilingual coverage is becoming increasingly important -- especially when monolingual resources are scarce. Recent studies have found that LLMs process multilingual inputs in shared concept spaces, thought to support generalization and cross-lingual transfer. However, these prior studies often do not use causal methods, lack deeper error analysis or focus on the final model only, leaving open how these spaces emerge during training. We investigate the development of language-agnostic concept spaces during pretraining of EuroLLM through the causal interpretability method of activation patching. We isolate cross-lingual concept representations, then inject them into a translation prompt to investigate how consistently translations can be altered, independently of the language. We find that shared concept spaces emerge early} and continue to refine, but that alignment with them is language-dependent}. Furthermore, in contrast to prior work, our fine-grained manual analysis reveals that some apparent gains in translation quality reflect shifts in behavior -- like selecting senses for polysemous words or translating instead of copying cross-lingual homographs -- rather than improved translation ability. Our findings offer new insight into the training dynamics of cross-lingual alignment and the conditions under which causal interpretability methods offer meaningful insights in multilingual contexts.

papers.title: Correctness-Optimized Residual Activation Lens (CORAL): Transferrable and Calibration-Aware Inference-Time Steering
papers.research_question: How can we improve both accuracy and calibration of LLMs during inference by directly steering using correctness signals from internal activations, rather than optimizing proxies?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CORAL, a lightweight inference-time steering method that uses regularized MLP probes on residual activations to improve accuracy and calibration in MCQA tasks, with demonstrated transferability across benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: CORAL provides a compute-efficient, transferable, and calibration-aware approach to improve MCQA performance during inference by extracting distributed correctness signals via regularized probes.
papers.key_findings:
CORAL consistently improves accuracy and calibration across three 7B models and multiple MCQA benchmarks.
CORAL's learned steering directions transfer without retraining to four held-out benchmarks, averaging 14% accuracy and 49% ECE improvements.
Correctness signals are distributed across many neurons and require supervised aggregation; sparse methods like SAE fail to capture them.
Middle layers (17-21) contain the most useful correctness signals for steering.
Regularized probes capture distributed correctness signals that sparse methods miss.
papers.limitation:
Limited to multiple-choice question answering; generalization to free-form generation is open.
Requires labeled data to train probes, which may not be available for all domains or languages.
Adds inference latency due to activation extraction and probe prediction.
Transfer performance depends on similarity between source and target tasks; dissimilar tasks yield smaller improvements.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit persistent miscalibration, especially after instruction tuning and preference alignment. Modified training objectives can improve calibration, but retraining is expensive. Inference-time steering offers a lightweight alternative, yet most existing methods optimize proxies for correctness rather than correctness itself. We introduce CORAL (Correctness-Optimized Residual Activation Lens), a regularized inference-time steering method that captures distributed correctness signals from model internal activations using weight-decay MLP probes. We evaluate CORAL across three 7B-parameter models and find that it consistently improves accuracy by 10\% and expected calibration error (ECE) by 50\% on average. We additionally demonstrate that these gains transfer without retraining to the complete published test sets of four held-out benchmarks (ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, Math-MC, OpenBookQA), averaging 14\% accuracy improvements and 49\% ECE improvements. Our results support the hypothesis that distributed information in model internals can be extracted using regularized probes when individual neurons are insufficient. CORAL thus provides a compute-efficient, transferable, and calibration-aware approach to improve MCQA performance during inference.

papers.title: Do Large Language Models Latently Perform Multi-Hop Reasoning?
papers.research_question: Do large language models perform latent multi-hop reasoning when completing two-hop prompts without explicit reasoning steps provided in the input?
papers.core_contribution: The paper establishes a framework to investigate latent multi-hop reasoning in LLMs, finding evidence that such reasoning exists for certain prompt types, with the first hop showing scaling with model size but the second hop not.
papers.conclusion: Latent multi-hop reasoning exists in LLMs but is highly contextual, with the first hop scaling with model size but the second hop not, indicating potential architectural or training limitations.
papers.key_findings:
Strong evidence for the first hop of reasoning: in about 70% of cases, changing the prompt to indirectly mention the bridge entity increases the model's internal recall of that entity.
Evidence for the second hop and overall traversal is weaker: in 60% of cases, increasing entity recall increases consistency between two-hop and one-hop prompt completions.
About 40% of the time both hops work together (compared to a 25% random baseline).
Up to 23% of fact composition types demonstrate strong evidence of latent multi-hop reasoning, occurring in more than 80% of cases.
The first hop of reasoning improves substantially with model size, but the second hop does not show clear scaling.
papers.limitation:
The analysis focuses on a narrow interpretation of the reasoning pathway, which in reality is likely more distributed across layers and tokens, so the observed effects might be a lower bound.
The study is limited to two-hop prompts and specific fact composition types.
papers.abstract: We study whether Large Language Models (LLMs) latently perform multi-hop reasoning with complex prompts such as "The mother of the singer of 'Superstition' is". We look for evidence of a latent reasoning pathway where an LLM (1) latently identifies "the singer of 'Superstition'" as Stevie Wonder, the bridge entity, and (2) uses its knowledge of Stevie Wonder's mother to complete the prompt. We analyze these two hops individually and consider their co-occurrence as indicative of latent multi-hop reasoning. For the first hop, we test if changing the prompt to indirectly mention the bridge entity instead of any other entity increases the LLM's internal recall of the bridge entity. For the second hop, we test if increasing this recall causes the LLM to better utilize what it knows about the bridge entity. We find strong evidence of latent multi-hop reasoning for the prompts of certain relation types, with the reasoning pathway used in more than 80% of the prompts. However, the utilization is highly contextual, varying across different types of prompts. Also, on average, the evidence for the second hop and the full multi-hop traversal is rather moderate and only substantial for the first hop. Moreover, we find a clear scaling trend with increasing model size for the first hop of reasoning but not for the second hop. Our experimental findings suggest potential challenges and opportunities for future development and applications of LLMs.

papers.title: Interpretable Visual Reasoning via Induced Symbolic Space
papers.research_question: How to induce visual concepts and their hierarchical relationships from question-answer pairs and images, and use them for interpretable visual reasoning.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces OCCAM, an object-centric visual reasoning framework that induces symbolic concepts and their hierarchy from question-answer pairs, achieving interpretable reasoning without human-annotated programs.
papers.conclusion: OCCAM achieves state-of-the-art visual reasoning and induces accurate, sufficient concepts for interpretable reasoning, enabling future extension to more sophisticated induction tasks.
papers.key_findings:
OCCAM achieves new state-of-the-art on CLEVR and GQA without external program supervision.
Induced concepts are sufficient for visual reasoning, with only ~1% performance drop when replacing visual features with concepts.
The induced concept hierarchy on CLEVR perfectly matches the data generator definition and human prior knowledge.
papers.limitation: Real-world data makes it difficult to induce some commonsense super concepts due to objects having multiple values for a concept (e.g., colors) and degrees of concepts.
future_direction: Extending concept induction to phrases, more complicated hierarchies, and degrees of features.
papers.abstract: We study the problem of concept induction in visual reasoning, i.e., identifying concepts and their hierarchical relationships from question-answer pairs associated with images; and achieve an interpretable model via working on the induced symbolic concept space. To this end, we first design a new framework named object-centric compositional attention model (OCCAM) to perform the visual reasoning task with object-level visual features. Then, we come up with a method to induce concepts of objects and relations using clues from the attention patterns between objects' visual features and question words. Finally, we achieve a higher level of interpretability by imposing OCCAM on the objects represented in the induced symbolic concept space. Our model design makes this an easy adaption via first predicting the concepts of objects and relations and then projecting the predicted concepts back to the visual feature space so the compositional reasoning module can process normally. Experiments on the CLEVR and GQA datasets demonstrate: 1) our OCCAM achieves a new state of the art without human-annotated functional programs; 2) our induced concepts are both accurate and sufficient as OCCAM achieves an on-par performance on objects represented either in visual features or in the induced symbolic concept space.

papers.title: Task Schema and Binding: A Double Dissociation Study of In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: Does in-context learning decompose into two separable mechanisms: Task Schema (abstract task type recognition) and Binding (specific input-output associations)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides causal mechanistic validation that in-context learning decomposes into two separable mechanisms—Task Schema (encoded in late MLP layers) and Binding (encoded in the residual stream)—and demonstrates a Prior-Schema trade-off where schema reliance inversely correlates with prior knowledge.
papers.conclusion: In-context learning operates through a compositional mechanism with two separable components (Task Schema and Binding), and the bottleneck for binding failures is attentional (recency bias) rather than output-level prior competition.
papers.key_findings:
Double dissociation: Task Schema transfers at 100% via late MLP patching; Binding transfers at 62% via residual stream patching, proving separable mechanisms.
Prior-Schema trade-off: Schema reliance inversely correlates with prior knowledge (Spearman ρ=-0.596, p<0.001).
Architecture generality: The Task Schema mechanism operates across all tested Transformer families and the non-Transformer Mamba model.
Binding failures are primarily due to recency-biased mis-attention (72.7%) and not prior competition (0%).
Task Schema is encoded in late MLP layers (75-95% network depth) and is robust to demonstration ordering.
papers.limitation:
Model scale: only tested up to 13B parameters; 70B+ and proprietary models remain untested.
Chain-of-thought (CoT) and multi-step reasoning are not tested.
Binding control is incomplete (62% success rate).
Prior measurement (zero-shot probability) is an imperfect proxy that may miss latent associations.
Ecological validity: controlled tasks may not fully represent real-world ICL with noisy demonstrations and ambiguous specifications.
future_direction: Testing larger models (70B+).
Investigating Chain-of-thought (CoT) and multi-step reasoning.
Improving binding control (e.g., via attention weight patching or activation steering).
papers.abstract: We provide causal mechanistic validation that in-context learning (ICL) decomposes into two separable mechanisms: Task Schema (abstract task type recognition) and Binding (specific input-output associations). Through activation patching experiments across 9 models from 7 Transformer families plus Mamba (370M-13B parameters), we establish three key findings: 1. Double dissociation: Task Schema transfers at 100% via late MLP patching; Binding transfers at 62% via residual stream patching -- proving separable mechanisms 2. Prior-Schema trade-off: Schema reliance inversely correlates with prior knowledge (Spearman rho = -0.596, p < 0.001, N=28 task-model pairs) 3. Architecture generality: The mechanism operates across all tested architectures including the non-Transformer Mamba These findings offer a mechanistic account of the ICL puzzle that contrasts with prior views treating ICL as a monolithic mechanism (whether retrieval-based, gradient descent-like, or purely Bayesian). By establishing that Schema and Binding are neurally dissociable -- not merely behavioral modes -- we provide causal evidence for dual-process theories of ICL. Models rely on Task Schema when prior knowledge is absent, but prior knowledge interferes through attentional mis-routing (72.7% recency bias) rather than direct output competition (0%). This explains why arbitrary mappings succeed (zero prior leads to full Schema reliance) while factual overrides fail -- and reveals that the true bottleneck is attentional, not output-level. Practical implications: Understanding these dual mechanisms enables more efficient prompt engineering -- reliable schema transfer reduces required demonstrations for novel tasks, while prior-aware design can mitigate the 38% binding failure rate in high-prior scenarios, improving ICL system reliability in production deployments.

papers.title: Contributions of Transformer Attention Heads in Multi- and Cross-lingual Tasks
papers.research_question: What are the effects of pruning attention heads in multilingual Transformer-based models on cross-lingual and multi-lingual tasks, and how can important heads be identified?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that pruning a subset of attention heads in multilingual Transformer models (mBERT and XLM-R) generally improves performance in cross-lingual and multi-lingual sequence labeling tasks, and introduces a gradient-based method to rank and identify which heads to prune.
papers.conclusion: Pruning attention heads in multilingual Transformer models generally improves performance in cross-lingual and multi-lingual sequence labeling tasks, and the gradient-based method effectively identifies heads to prune, offering better model interpretability and efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Pruning attention heads in mBERT and XLM-R generally has positive effects on model performance in cross-lingual and multi-lingual sequence labeling tasks (POS, NER, SF).
A gradient-based method can effectively rank attention heads by importance, and pruning the lowest-ranked heads leads to performance improvements.
The important attention heads for a task are shared across languages, as evidenced by high correlation in head rankings across different languages.
Pruning attention heads is beneficial even when training data in the target language is limited, making models more applicable to resource-poor languages.
In multi-source language settings, pruning attention heads also improves performance, and the gradient-based ranking method can be extended to multiple source languages.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to sequence labeling tasks (POS, NER, SF) and may not generalize to other cross-lingual tasks.
future_direction: Improving model interpretability in other cross-lingual and multi-lingual tasks, e.g., XNLI and other passage-level classification tasks.
papers.abstract: Weicheng Ma, Kai Zhang, Renze Lou, Lili Wang, Soroush Vosoughi. Proceedings of the 59th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics and the 11th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2021.

papers.title: LLMs Process Lists With General Filter Heads
papers.research_question: How do LLMs implement list-processing tasks, particularly filtering operations, and what are the mechanisms behind them?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs implement list-filtering operations via specialized attention heads (filter heads) that encode predicates as geometric directions in query space, enabling portable and general filtering across different formats, languages, and tasks.
papers.conclusion: Transformer LMs develop human-interpretable implementations of abstract computational operations that generalize in ways similar to strategies used in traditional functional programming patterns.
papers.key_findings:
Filter heads encode predicates in their query states and attend to items satisfying the predicate, implementing a lazy evaluation strategy.
The predicate representation in filter heads is abstract and portable: it can be transferred across different collections, presentation formats, languages, and even different filter-reduce tasks.
LLMs also employ an eager evaluation strategy for filtering by storing is_match flags directly in item representations, revealing computational redundancy.
Ablation of filter heads causes significant performance drops in selection tasks, confirming their necessity, while they are distinct from other specialized head types like Function Vector and Concept Induction heads.
Filter heads are concentrated in middle layers and are shared across different predicates, forming a general filtering mechanism.
papers.limitation:
Task coverage limited to six filter-reduce tasks, which may not capture the full diversity of filtering strategies in LLMs.
Only tested on four models (Llama and Gemma families), so the findings may not generalize to other architectures or smaller models where parameter constraints might lead to different implementations.
Validation based on first token prediction may restrict the scope of tasks that can be studied and may not capture full model behavior.
papers.abstract: We investigate the mechanisms underlying a range of list-processing tasks in LLMs, and we find that LLMs have learned to encode a compact, causal representation of a general filtering operation that mirrors the generic "filter" function of functional programming. Using causal mediation analysis on a diverse set of list-processing tasks, we find that a small number of attention heads, which we dub filter heads, encode a compact representation of the filtering predicate in their query states at certain tokens. We demonstrate that this predicate representation is general and portable: it can be extracted and reapplied to execute the same filtering operation on different collections, presented in different formats, languages, or even in tasks. However, we also identify situations where transformer LMs can exploit a different strategy for filtering: eagerly evaluating if an item satisfies the predicate and storing this intermediate result as a flag directly in the item representations. Our results reveal that transformer LMs can develop human-interpretable implementations of abstract computational operations that generalize in ways that are surprisingly similar to strategies used in traditional functional programming patterns.

papers.title: Probing Linguistic Information for Logical Inference in Pre-trained Language Models
papers.research_question: Do pre-trained language models encode linguistic information essential to symbolic inference systems? Do they acquire new linguistic information for inference during fine-tuning for the NLI task?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a probing methodology to assess linguistic information for logical inference in pre-trained language models, finding that they encode some but not all types of information, and that fine-tuning can help acquire missing information.
papers.conclusion: Pre-trained language models encode some linguistic information for inference, with more on simple than complex phenomena, and can acquire additional information through fine-tuning, showing potential as knowledge bases for symbolic reasoning systems.
papers.key_findings:
Pre-trained language models encode more information on simple semantic phenomena (e.g., lexical alignment, contradiction signatures) than on complex phenomena (e.g., monotonicity, sentiment and relational knowledge alignment).
Linear classifiers may misinterpret semantic information, while MLP classifiers achieve higher accuracy and similar selectivity, suggesting that more expressive probes are needed for semantic tasks.
Label-wise analysis shows that the amount of linguistic information encoded varies across labels, with models performing better on some labels than others.
Pre-trained language models can learn some missing linguistic information (e.g., for sentiment and relational-knowledge alignment) through fine-tuning on NLI data, but not for monotonicity.
Pre-trained language models encode significantly more linguistic information for inference than baseline word embeddings, as measured by information gain.
papers.limitation:
Even high expressive classifiers like MLP fail to perform well on tasks with monotonicity and higher-level semantic reasoning.
The training data of MultiNLI may not contain enough examples about monotonicity, which could explain why fine-tuning does not improve performance on monotonicity polarization.
future_direction: Conduct further analysis on each type of linguistic information in language models by constructing more detailed probing datasets.
Design logical systems that can access linguistic information from pre-trained language models and apply them in the inference process for improved performance on large benchmarks.
papers.abstract: Progress in pre-trained language models has led to a surge of impressive results on downstream tasks for natural language understanding. Recent work on probing pre-trained language models uncovered a wide range of linguistic properties encoded in their contextualized representations. However, it is unclear whether they encode semantic knowledge that is crucial to symbolic inference methods. We propose a methodology for probing knowledge for inference that logical systems require but often lack in pre-trained language model representations. Our probing datasets cover a list of key types of knowledge used by many symbolic inference systems. We find that (i) pre-trained language models do encode several types of knowledge for inference, but there are also some types of knowledge for inference that are not encoded, (ii) language models can effectively learn missing knowledge for inference through fine-tuning. Overall, our findings provide insights into which aspects of knowledge for inference language models and their pre-training procedures capture. Moreover, we have demonstrated language models' potential as semantic and background knowledge bases for supporting symbolic inference methods.

papers.title: Beyond English-Centric LLMs: What Language Do Multilingual Language Models Think in?
papers.research_question: What internal latent language do non-English-centric large language models use in their intermediate layers when processing tasks?
papers.core_contribution: This study demonstrates that the internal latent language of LLMs is determined by their training corpora, with Japanese-specific models using Japanese as a latent language. For non-dominant target languages, models activate the latent language most closely related to it, and the transition from latent to target language occurs in sparse dimensions related to language identity.
papers.conclusion: The internal latent language of LLMs is majorly determined by the language of its training corpora. The transition from latent to target language involves sparse dimensions related to language identity, providing insights for understanding model performance.
papers.key_findings:
Japanese-specific models (Swallow, LLM-jp) use Japanese as an internal latent language when processing Japanese, unlike English-centric Llama-2.
When processing non-dominant languages (French, Chinese), Swallow and LLM-jp exhibit dual internal latent languages (English and Japanese), preferring the one more closely related to the target language.
In culture-conflict QA tasks, intermediate layers initially produce answers biased by the culture of the internal latent language before aligning with the target language context.
The shift from internal latent language to target language representation occurs only in sparse dimensions of the hidden vectors, which are inferred to be related to language identity.
papers.limitation: An exception in Swallow's translation results (higher Japanese probability for French target than Chinese) may be due to specific content in its training corpus, but this hypothesis is difficult to verify.
future_direction: Extend investigation to models with other specific dominant languages, such as Chinese, French, and Arabic.
papers.abstract: In this study, we investigate whether non-English-centric LLMs, despite their strong performance, `think' in their respective dominant language: more precisely, `think' refers to how the representations of intermediate layers, when un-embedded into the vocabulary space, exhibit higher probabilities for certain dominant languages during generation. We term such languages as internal $\textbf{latent languages}$. We examine the latent language of three typical categories of models for Japanese processing: Llama2, an English-centric model; Swallow, an English-centric model with continued pre-training in Japanese; and LLM-jp, a model pre-trained on balanced English and Japanese corpora. Our empirical findings reveal that, unlike Llama2 which relies exclusively on English as the internal latent language, Japanese-specific Swallow and LLM-jp employ both Japanese and English, exhibiting dual internal latent languages. For any given target language, the model preferentially activates the latent language most closely related to it. In addition, we explore how intermediate layers respond to questions involving cultural conflicts between latent internal and target output languages. We further explore how the language identity shifts across layers while keeping consistent semantic meaning reflected in the intermediate layer representations. This study deepens the understanding of non-English-centric large language models, highlighting the intricate dynamics of language representation within their intermediate layers.

papers.title: Fine-Tuning is Subgraph Search: A New Lens on Learning Dynamics
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how fine-tuning works from a mechanistic interpretability perspective, viewing fine-tuning as a search for and optimization of a subgraph within the model's computational graph.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces circuit-tuning, a fine-tuning method that dynamically localizes and optimizes subgraphs (circuits) within a model's computational graph, enabling analysis of learning dynamics and balancing task performance with general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Circuit-tuning provides a new method for studying learning dynamics from a mechanistic interpretability perspective, offering insights into how fine-tuning works and enabling more precise fine-tuning that balances task performance and general capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit-tuning provides better training stability and preserves language modeling ability better than full fine-tuning.
The functionality of specific attention heads (Subject Attribute Heads) can reverse during fine-tuning to adapt to new tasks.
Some attention heads (Subject Identification Heads) preserve their functions and are shared before and after fine-tuning.
Nodes within a circuit cooperate through division of labor and indirect interactions to complete tasks.
Edges in the computational graph exhibit strengthening and weakening akin to Hebbian learning during fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: The study of mechanistic interpretability aims to reverse-engineer a model to explain its behaviors. While recent studies have focused on the static mechanism of a certain behavior, the learning dynamics inside a model remain to be explored. In this work, we develop a fine-tuning method for analyzing the mechanism behind learning. Inspired by the concept of intrinsic dimension, we view a model as a computational graph with redundancy for a specific task, and treat the fine-tuning process as a search for and optimization of a subgraph within this graph. Based on this hypothesis, we propose circuit-tuning, an algorithm that iteratively builds the subgraph for a specific task and updates the relevant parameters in a heuristic way. We first validate our hypothesis through a carefully designed experiment and provide a detailed analysis of the learning dynamics during fine-tuning. Subsequently, we conduct experiments on more complex tasks, demonstrating that circuit-tuning could strike a balance between the performance on the target task and the general capabilities. Our work offers a new analytical method for the dynamics of fine-tuning, provides new findings on the mechanisms behind the training process, and inspires the design of superior algorithms for the training of neural networks.

papers.title: The Truth is in There: Improving Reasoning in Language Models with Layer-Selective Rank Reduction
papers.research_question: Can selectively removing higher-order components of weight matrices in Transformer models improve performance on reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Selectively removing higher-order components of weight matrices via low-rank approximation (LASER) improves LLM performance on reasoning tasks, especially for less frequent facts, by denoising conflicting responses encoded in higher-order components.
papers.conclusion: LASER is an effective post-hoc intervention that improves reasoning by denoising weight matrices, and its success warrants further study on why higher-order components accumulate noise.
papers.key_findings:
LASER improves accuracy on various NLP benchmarks, with the largest gains on facts less frequent in training data.
Improvements are most pronounced when reducing rank in later MLP layers, while early layer reduction harms performance.
LASER increases model robustness to paraphrases of questions.
Higher-order components often encode noisy or conflicting responses (e.g., generic high-frequency words or incorrect answers of the same semantic type).
Composing LASER interventions across multiple layers yields further performance improvements.
papers.limitation:
LASER slightly increases perplexity on the training data, indicating a trade-off between task performance and language modeling fluency.
The improvements in non-text domains (e.g., reinforcement learning) are smaller and less consistent.
future_direction: Understanding why higher-order components in weight matrices accumulate noisy answers during training.
Investigating the effect of model architecture and other structural choices on the occurrence of this phenomenon.
Explaining why the phenomenon is specifically true for later layers in the MLP.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs) have become a fixture in modern machine learning. Correspondingly, significant resources are allocated towards research that aims to further advance this technology, typically resulting in models of increasing size that are trained on increasing amounts of data. This work, however, demonstrates the surprising result that it is often possible to significantly improve the performance of LLMs by selectively removing higher-order components of their weight matrices. This simple intervention, which we call LAyer-SElective Rank reduction (LASER), can be done on a model after training has completed, and requires no additional parameters or data. We show extensive experiments demonstrating the generality of this finding across language models and datasets, and provide in-depth analyses offering insights into both when LASER is effective and the mechanism by which it operates.

papers.title: Exploring the LLM Journey from Cognition to Expression with Linear Representations
papers.research_question: How do cognitive and expressive capabilities develop and interact in large language models across pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning from human feedback stages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that cognitive capabilities in LLMs are established during pretraining, while expressive capabilities develop during SFT and RLHF, with cognitive capability setting an upper bound for expressive capability.
papers.conclusion: This research reveals the potential connection between the hidden space and the output space, contributing valuable insights into the interpretability and controllability of LLM training processes.
papers.key_findings:
Cognitive capability is primarily established during the pretraining stage, whereas expressive capability develops during SFT and RLHF.
There is a strong statistical correlation between cognitive and expressive capabilities, with cognitive capability acting as an upper bound.
The gap between cognitive and expressive capabilities can be bridged by optimization-free methods such as few-shot learning and repeated sampling.
The vocabulary linear layer plays a crucial role in expressive capability, and its training during SFT/RLHF helps reduce the gap.
Layer-wise analysis reveals a plateau in cognitive capability in deeper layers, indicating redundancy in the model architecture.
future_direction: Exploring additional linear analysis techniques for model analysis and control.
papers.abstract: This paper presents an in-depth examination of the evolution and interplay of cognitive and expressive capabilities in large language models (LLMs), with a specific focus on Baichuan-7B and Baichuan-33B, an advanced bilingual (Chinese and English) LLM series. We define and explore the model's cognitive and expressive capabilities through linear representations across three critical phases: Pretraining, Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), and Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). Cognitive capability is defined as the quantity and quality of information conveyed by the neuron output vectors within the network, similar to the neural signal processing in human cognition. Expressive capability is defined as the model's capability to produce word-level output. Our findings unveil a sequential development pattern, where cognitive abilities are largely established during Pretraining, whereas expressive abilities predominantly advance during SFT and RLHF. Statistical analyses confirm a significant correlation between the two capabilities, suggesting that cognitive capacity may limit expressive potential. The paper also explores the theoretical underpinnings of these divergent developmental trajectories and their connection to the LLMs' architectural design. Moreover, we evaluate various optimization-independent strategies, such as few-shot learning and repeated sampling, which bridge the gap between cognitive and expressive capabilities. This research reveals the potential connection between the hidden space and the output space, contributing valuable insights into the interpretability and controllability of their training processes.

papers.title: A Reply to Makelov et al. (2023)'s "Interpretability Illusion" Arguments
papers.research_question: Are the phenomena identified by Makelov et al. (2023) as 'interpretability illusions' actually inherent properties of distributed representations in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that the 'interpretability illusions' identified by Makelov et al. (2023) are not illusions but inherent properties of distributed representations, and provides additional experiments using DAS to analyze causal mechanisms in GPT-2.
papers.conclusion: The phenomena labeled as 'interpretability illusions' are inherent to distributed representations, and the work by Makelov et al. (2023) has advanced the field of mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Even directions considered non-illusory by Makelov et al. can be classified as illusory under their own definition.
The illusions reported by Makelov et al. are artifacts of their training and evaluation paradigms.
DAS can reproduce and extend findings on the IOI task, showing that name position information in GPT-2 is distributed across attention heads and emerges in the 8th layer.
Name position information is not carried by MLP activations but by the self-attention block in the 8th layer.
The correct IO name representation is distributed across multiple attention heads in the 9th layer.
papers.abstract: We respond to the recent paper by Makelov et al. (2023), which reviews subspace interchange intervention methods like distributed alignment search (DAS; Geiger et al. 2023) and claims that these methods potentially cause "interpretability illusions". We first review Makelov et al. (2023)'s technical notion of what an "interpretability illusion" is, and then we show that even intuitive and desirable explanations can qualify as illusions in this sense. As a result, their method of discovering "illusions" can reject explanations they consider "non-illusory". We then argue that the illusions Makelov et al. (2023) see in practice are artifacts of their training and evaluation paradigms. We close by emphasizing that, though we disagree with their core characterization, Makelov et al. (2023)'s examples and discussion have undoubtedly pushed the field of interpretability forward.

papers.title: Steering Knowledge Selection Behaviours in LLMs via SAE-Based Representation Engineering
papers.research_question: How can we control the knowledge selection behavior of large language models (LLMs) when there is a conflict between their parametric knowledge and contextual knowledge at inference time?
papers.core_contribution: This paper proposes SPARE, a training-free representation engineering method that uses pre-trained sparse auto-encoders (SAEs) to identify and edit functional features in the hidden states of LLMs, enabling precise control over knowledge selection behavior during inference to resolve context-memory conflicts.
papers.conclusion: SPARE provides an effective and efficient training-free method for controlling knowledge selection in LLMs at inference time, offering a promising approach to managing knowledge conflicts without significant computational overhead.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge conflicts can be detected by probing the residual stream of LLMs, with the strongest signal appearing in mid-layers.
SPARE effectively steers LLMs to use either contextual or parametric knowledge, outperforming existing representation engineering and contrastive decoding methods.
The residual stream exhibits a significantly more skewed representation when the model uses contextual knowledge compared to when it uses parametric knowledge.
SPARE requires editing only a very small set of SAE features (e.g., less than 0.05% for Gemma2-9B) to achieve control.
The method is more effective at changing the model's behavior from using contextual to parametric knowledge than other inference-time methods.
papers.limitation:
The approach relies on pre-trained SAEs, so it may not apply to models where such SAEs are unavailable or cannot be efficiently trained.
The experiments are conducted on specific open-domain QA tasks; generalization to other task types (e.g., complex reasoning, long-form generation) is unclear.
Control is evaluated primarily in a binary fashion (contextual vs. parametric knowledge), whereas real-world decisions may require more nuanced approaches.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can store a significant amount of factual knowledge in their parameters. However, their parametric knowledge may conflict with the information provided in the context -- this phenomenon, known as \emph{context-memory knowledge conflicts}, can lead to undesirable model behaviour, such as reliance on outdated or incorrect information. Analysing the internal activations of LLMs, we find that they can internally register the signals of knowledge conflict at mid-layers. Such signals allow us to detect whether a knowledge conflict occurs and use \emph{inference-time} intervention strategies to resolve it. In this work, we propose \textsc{SpARE}, a \emph{training-free} representation engineering method that uses pre-trained sparse auto-encoders (SAEs) to control the knowledge selection behaviour of LLMs. \textsc{SpARE} identifies the functional features that control the knowledge selection behaviours and applies them to edit the internal activations of LLMs at inference time. Our experimental results show that \textsc{SpARE} can effectively control the usage of either knowledge source to resolve knowledge conflict in open-domain question-answering tasks, surpassing existing representation engineering methods ($+10\%$) as well as contrastive decoding methods ($+15\%$).

papers.title: Echoes of BERT: Do Modern Language Models Rediscover the Classical NLP Pipeline?
papers.research_question: How do modern language models encode linguistic structure, and do they rediscover the classical NLP pipeline observed in earlier models like BERT?
papers.core_contribution: Modern language models rediscover the classical NLP pipeline, with lexical information concentrated in early layers and becoming nonlinear, while inflectional morphology remains linearly accessible across layers and languages.
papers.conclusion: Modern transformer language models rediscover the classical NLP pipeline and exhibit robust representational regularities for lexical and inflectional information across architectures, sizes, and languages.
papers.key_findings:
Modern LMs consistently organize linguistic information hierarchically: early layers process syntax, middle layers handle semantics and entities, later layers capture discourse.
Lexical identity (lemma) information is most accessible in early layers and becomes increasingly nonlinear deeper in the network.
Inflectional morphology remains highly linearly accessible across all layers and across six typologically diverse languages.
These representational patterns emerge early during pretraining and are robust across model architectures, sizes, and training regimes.
Inflectional features occupy compact, linearly accessible subspaces in the residual stream, enabling effective steering interventions.
papers.limitation:
Representation extraction for decoder-only models uses the final subword token, which may not be optimal for all architectures.
The study does not explicitly examine cases where different grammatical functions share the same surface form (e.g., infinitive and non-past verb forms).
Classifiers only detect correlations in hidden activations, not causal mechanisms.
Steering experiments measure changes in classifier performance rather than downstream model outputs.
future_direction: Develop better extraction methods for word representations from decoder-only models.
Examine how models separate form from function across languages in cases of surface-form ambiguity.
Design more complex experiments to evaluate steering effects on actual model generation.
papers.abstract: Large transformer-based language models dominate modern NLP, yet our understanding of how they encode linguistic information relies primarily on studies of early models like BERT and GPT-2. Building on classic BERTology work, we analyze 25 models spanning from classical architectures (BERT, DeBERTa, GPT-2) to modern large language models (Pythia, OLMo-2, Gemma-2, Qwen2.5, Llama-3.1), probing layer-by-layer representations across eight linguistic tasks in English. Consistent with earlier findings, we find that hierarchical organization persists in modern models: early layers capture syntax, middle layers handle semantics and entity-level information, and later layers encode discourse phenomena. We dive deeper, conducting an in-depth multilingual analysis of two specific linguistic properties - lexical identity and inflectional morphology - that help disentangle form from meaning. We find that lexical information concentrates linearly in early layers but becomes increasingly nonlinear deeper in the network, while inflectional information remains linearly accessible throughout all layers. Additional analyses of attention mechanisms, steering vectors, and pretraining checkpoints reveal where this information resides within layers, how it can be functionally manipulated, and how representations evolve during pretraining. Taken together, our findings suggest that, even with substantial advances in LLM technologies, transformer models learn to organize linguistic information in similar ways, regardless of model architecture, size, or training regime, indicating that these properties are important for next token prediction. Our code is available at https://github.com/ml5885/model_internal_sleuthing

papers.title: The Hydra Effect: Emergent Self-repair in Language Model Computations
papers.research_question: What is the internal computational structure of language models, and how do they respond to ablations? The paper investigates self-repair mechanisms (Hydra effect) and erasure functions in MLP layers.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies two internal self-repair motifs in language models: the Hydra effect (downstream attention layers compensate for ablated layers) and erasure by late MLP layers (which downregulate the maximum-likelihood token).
papers.conclusion: The Hydra effect and erasure MLPs complicate circuit-level attribution and have implications for interpretability research, suggesting that assigning semantics to MLP neurons may be more difficult and that ablation studies must account for downstream compensatory changes.
papers.key_findings:
Language models exhibit the Hydra effect: ablating an attention layer causes a downstream attention layer to increase its impact to compensate.
Late MLP layers have an erasure function, acting to downregulate the maximum-likelihood token, and this effect is attenuated when attention layers are ablated.
Direct (unembedding-based) and total (ablation-based) importance measures are poorly correlated in most layers, except late layers.
The compensatory response is highly correlated with changes in direct effect at intermediate layers, explaining up to 92% of variance at layer 23.
These self-repair effects occur even in models trained without dropout, suggesting they are inherent to the architecture or training.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is performed at the layer level and does not investigate finer-grained components like individual attention heads or activation directions.
The compensatory effect does not fully restore the output, indicating that ablations still have a nonzero total effect.
future_direction: How much does the Hydra effect occur across the entire training distribution? Does sequence length play any role?
What are the Hydra effect attention heads responding to in the residual stream?
Do the same downstream heads act as Hydra effect replacement heads across multiple contexts?
papers.abstract: We investigate the internal structure of language model computations using causal analysis and demonstrate two motifs: (1) a form of adaptive computation where ablations of one attention layer of a language model cause another layer to compensate (which we term the Hydra effect) and (2) a counterbalancing function of late MLP layers that act to downregulate the maximum-likelihood token. Our ablation studies demonstrate that language model layers are typically relatively loosely coupled (ablations to one layer only affect a small number of downstream layers). Surprisingly, these effects occur even in language models trained without any form of dropout. We analyse these effects in the context of factual recall and consider their implications for circuit-level attribution in language models.

papers.title: Kinbank: A global database of kinship terminology
papers.abstract: For a single species, human kinship organization is both remarkably diverse and strikingly organized. Kinship terminology is the structured vocabulary used to classify, refer to, and address relatives and family. Diversity in kinship terminology has been analyzed by anthropologists for over 150 years, although recurrent patterning across cultures remains incompletely explained. Despite the wealth of kinship data in the anthropological record, comparative studies of kinship terminology are hindered by data accessibility. Here we present Kinbank, a new database of 210,903 kinterms from a global sample of 1,229 spoken languages. Using open-access and transparent data provenance, Kinbank offers an extensible resource for kinship terminology, enabling researchers to explore the rich diversity of human family organization and to test longstanding hypotheses about the origins and drivers of recurrent patterns. We illustrate our contribution with two examples. We demonstrate strong gender bias in the phonological structure of parent terms across 1,022 languages, and we show that there is no evidence for a coevolutionary relationship between cross-cousin marriage and bifurcate-merging terminology in Bantu languages. Analysing kinship data is notoriously challenging; Kinbank aims to eliminate data accessibility issues from that challenge and provide a platform to build an interdisciplinary understanding of kinship.

papers.title: universals and rule options in kinship terminology: a synthesis of three formal approaches
papers.abstract: Extension rules, relational analysis, and componential analysis are integrated into a new generative model of kinship terminology focusing on the universal aspects of kin‐term systems. Widely divergent consanguineal systems (Crow‐Omaha, Dravidian, Iroquois, and Eskimo) are shown to share a substantial core of rules and to display virtually identical relationships between superordinate categories. Tax's rule of uniform reciprocals applies without exception at the proper level of abstraction. Primary differences between systems, such as cross! parallel phenomena, follow from the interaction of universal rules with a small number of rule options . [kinship terminology, universals, generative model, extension rules, relational analysis, componential analysis]

papers.title: The global recurrence and variability of kinship terminology structure
papers.abstract: The extent to which kinship terminology varies between linguistic groups is a long-debated but unresolved social and linguistic puzzle. Contemporary research shows that a six-category typology is overly simplistic, but no alternatives have reached broad acceptance. This paper takes a data-driven solution to this problem. Using data from the release of Kinbank, a global database of 1,156 kinship terminology, I quantitatively review the global diversity of kinship terminology to derive a more granular typology of kinship terminology. In a two-part analysis, I show that kinship terminology structure is more diverse than is often assumed across three metrics. Firstly, more than six types are needed to represent the global diversity of kinship terminology. Secondly, typological categories are not equally variable. Some categories may contain identically structured terminology. Others may contain languages that only share a single feature. Finally, different subsets of kin (e.g. cousins vs grandparents) show different levels of variability. In the second part of the analysis, I explore the global distribution of the new typological categories, identifying globally and locally recurring structures. My analysis demonstrates how data can carve this semantic domain at its joints to identify observed clusters of diversity.

papers.title: No universals in the cultural evolution of kinship terminology
papers.abstract: Kinship terminologies are the semantic systems of language that express kinship relations between individuals: in English, 'aunt' denotes a parent's sister. Theoretical models of kinship terminology diversity reduce over 10 billion possible organisations to six key types, each of which are hypothesised to be aligned with particular cultural norms of descent, marriage or residence patterns (Murdock, 1949). Often, terminological type is used to infer social patterns in past societies based on these putative relationships between kinship terminologies and social structure, and these associations are staples of 'Anthropology 101'. However, these relationships have not been scrutinised using modern comparative methods. Here we show that kinship terminologies vertically track language phylogeny in Austronesian, Bantu, and Uto-Aztecan, three languages families of different time-depths and environments. We find no unidirectional or universal models of evolution in kinship terminology. Of 18 existing anthropological coevolutionary theories regarding kinship terminology and cultural practices across 176 societies, we find only patchy support, and no evidence for putative universal drivers of evolution in kinship terminologies.

papers.title: Efficient communication drives the semantic structure of kinship terminology
papers.abstract: Semantic distinctions are encoded variably in kinship terminology, the set of words that denotes family members. Nonetheless, it has been suggested that kinship terminology, like other linguistic domains, is constrained by opposing pressures to be simple yet expressive. Here, we use this insight to explore how the meaning space for kinship is structured cross-linguistically. Under the assumption that kinship systems map forms to meanings in a compressible, structure-preserving manner, we designed a metric for identifying which semantic features are most important for distinguishing individuals in a kinship system. For 1229 kinship systems, we calculated the correlation between semantic similarity (the weighted sum of shared semantic features between individuals) and wordform similarity (the edit similarity between terms). We then identified the optimal weight for each semantic feature in each language, confirming that kinship systems vary in which semantic features they encode, and that the features themselves vary in the extent to which they are encoded.
